summary.text: Explicit finite witness computations establish Goldbach representations through 8012 and Lemoine representations through 15727; above those bounds, positivity supplies primes \(q,q+6,p,p-6\) with \(n=p+q\) for even \(n\) and \(n=p+2q\) for odd \(n\). For any bound \(N\), applying the even case to \(n=2(N+4007)\) yields the cousin-prime pair \((p-6,p)\) with \(p-6>N\), so such pairs are unbounded and hence infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. The sequence term \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) is the number of natural numbers \(q<n\) satisfying
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\[
 q,\quad q+6,\quad n-c(n)q,\quad n-c(n)q-6
\]
are all prime. If we put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q,
\]
then the inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) says precisely that \(p>q\), and these are exactly the representations described in the statement.

Assume throughout the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(a(n)>0\).

We prove Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs.

First, we record the finite calculations needed below the two thresholds. Their construction and validation are as follows.

For Goldbach, every even integer \(n\) with
\[
4\le n\le 8012
\]
was assigned a prime \(q<256\) for which \(n-q\) is prime. The assignments were divided into blocks. For \(j=0,1,\ldots,79\), block \(j\) consists of the fifty even numbers
\[
 4+100j,\ 6+100j,\ldots,\ 102+100j.
\]
The last block consists of
\[
8004,8006,8008,8010,8012.
\]
Within a block beginning at \(s\), its fifty choices \(q_0,\ldots,q_{49}\) were stored as the base-\(256\) integer
\[
 C=\sum_{i=0}^{49}q_i256^i;
\]
for the final block the analogous sum has five digits. Successive extraction of the remainder modulo \(256\), followed by division by \(256\), recovers the choices. Direct trial division of the recovered numbers gives, for every relevant index \(i\),
\[
 q_i\text{ prime},\qquad s+2i-q_i\text{ prime}.
\]
Consequently, with \(p_i=s+2i-q_i\),
\[
 s+2i=p_i+q_i
\]
is a sum of two primes. Hence
\[
\tag{G_f}
\text{every even }n\text{ with }4\le n\le8012\text{ is a sum of two primes.}
\]

For Lemoine, the same kind of table was made for every odd integer \(n\) with
\[
7\le n\le15727.
\]
For \(j=0,1,\ldots,156\), block \(j\) consists of the fifty odd numbers
\[
7+100j,\ 9+100j,\ldots,\ 105+100j,
\]
and the final block consists of
\[
15707,15709,\ldots,15727.
\]
For each block beginning at \(s\), base-\(256\) digits \(q_i<256\) were checked to satisfy
\[
 q_i\text{ prime},\qquad s+2i-2q_i\text{ prime}.
\]
Thus, putting \(p_i=s+2i-2q_i\), one obtains
\[
 s+2i=p_i+2q_i
\]
with \(p_i,q_i\) prime. Therefore
\[
\tag{L_f}
\text{every odd }n\text{ with }7\le n\le15727\text{ has the form }p+2q
\]
with \(p,q\) prime.

For completeness, the primality checks in these two finite computations use the following elementary criterion. For an integer \(m\le40000\), first accept \(m=2\). Otherwise require \(m>2\) and odd, and test the odd possible divisors
\[
3,5,7,\ldots,261,
\]
stopping as soon as the square of the candidate divisor exceeds \(m\). If none of the tested numbers whose square is at most \(m\) divides \(m\), then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, if \(m>1\) were composite, it would have a divisor \(d\) with
\[
2\le d\le\sqrt m.
\]
Since \(m\) has already been required to be odd, such a divisor may be taken odd. Also \(\sqrt m\le200\), so all relevant odd divisors occur in the displayed trial-division range. This proves the soundness of every primality decision used in the tables. All quantities checked in the Goldbach and Lemoine tables are below \(40000\). Notice also that if \(n-q\) is prime, then it is at least \(2\), so the natural-number subtraction has not lost information and \(n=(n-q)+q\). Similarly, if \(n-2q\) is prime, then it is at least \(2\), and hence \(n=(n-2q)+2q\). Thus the finite calculations establish exactly \((G_f)\) and \((L_f)\), rather than merely truncated-subtraction identities.

We next extract the mathematical consequence of positivity of \(a(n)\).

Suppose \(n>8012\) is even. By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\). Since \(a(n)\) is the cardinality of the finite set of admissible values of \(q\), that set is nonempty. Choose one of its elements \(q\). Since \(n\) is even, \(n\bmod2=0\), so \(c(n)=1\). The defining conditions become
\[
 2q<n,
\]
and
\[
 q,\quad q+6,\quad n-q,\quad n-q-6
\]
are prime. We shall use this consequence in the form
\[
\tag{E}
\exists q:\quad 2q<n,
\quad q,q+6,n-q,n-q-6\text{ are prime}.
\]

Similarly, suppose \(n>15727\) is odd. Then \(a(n)>0\), so an admissible \(q\) exists. This time \(n\bmod2=1\), hence \(c(n)=2\). Therefore
\[
 3q<n,
\]
and
\[
 q,\quad q+6,\quad n-2q,\quad n-2q-6
\]
are prime. Thus
\[
\tag{O}
\exists q:\quad 3q<n,
\quad q,q+6,n-2q,n-2q-6\text{ are prime}.
\]

We now prove Goldbach's conjecture. Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), the finite result \((G_f)\) supplies primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+q\).

If \(n>8012\), apply \((E)\) and choose the resulting \(q\). Set
\[
 p=n-q.
\]
The conditions in \((E)\) state that both \(p=n-q\) and \(q\) are prime. Moreover, \(2q<n\) in particular implies \(q<n\), so subtraction is ordinary subtraction and
\[
 n=(n-q)+q=p+q.
\]
Thus every even integer at least \(4\) is a sum of two primes. This is Goldbach's conjecture in the required form.

Next we prove Lemoine's conjecture. Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again there are two cases.

If \(n\le15727\), the finite result \((L_f)\) supplies primes \(p,q\) with
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]

If \(n>15727\), apply \((O)\). For its value of \(q\), put
\[
 p=n-2q.
\]
Both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime by \((O)\). The inequality \(3q<n\) implies \(2q<n\), so
\[
 n=(n-2q)+2q=p+2q.
\]
Hence every odd integer at least \(7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, which is Lemoine's conjecture.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many primes \(r\) for which \(r+6\) is prime. We prove that such primes are unbounded.

Let \(N\) be an arbitrary natural number. Define
\[
 n=2(N+4007)=2N+8014.
\]
Then \(n\) is even and \(n>8012\). Apply \((E)\) to this \(n\), obtaining \(q\) such that
\[
2q<n
\]
and both \(n-q\) and \(n-q-6\) are prime. Define
\[
 r=n-q-6.
\]
Then \(r\) is prime. Since a prime is at least \(2\), the statement that \(n-q-6\) is prime guarantees \(n-q\ge8\), so no truncation is involved and
\[
 r+6=n-q.
\]
The latter number is also prime. Thus \((r,r+6)\) is a cousin-prime pair.

We must show that its first member exceeds the prescribed bound \(N\). From \(2q<n=2N+8014\), and integrality, one has
\[
 q\le N+4006.
\]
Therefore
\[
 r=2N+8014-q-6
   \ge 2N+8008-(N+4006)
   =N+4002>N.
\]
So for every \(N\) there is a prime \(r>N\) such that \(r+6\) is prime. The set
\[
\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}
\]
is therefore unbounded. Every finite set of natural numbers is bounded by its maximum, so this unbounded set must be infinite.

We have proved, from the assumed positivity of \(A219055(n)\) above the stated even and odd thresholds, Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs \((p,p+6)\), as required.
